options.a: Mortgage loans insured by federal agencies
options.b: Construction loans made to homebuilders
options.c: Direct ownership of a single rental property
options.d: Real estate cash flows via a pooled security

distractorExplanations.a: Agency-insured mortgages describe GNMA pass-throughs, not REITs.
distractorExplanations.b: Some mortgage REITs lend, but REITs mainly give pooled real estate exposure.
distractorExplanations.c: REIT holders own shares in a portfolio, not title to a property.

options.a: Has voting rights but is paid after common holders
options.b: Gets dividend priority over common, with limited votes
options.c: Pays variable dividends that rise with earnings
options.d: Ranks ahead of bondholders when a corporation is liquidated

distractorExplanations.d: Reverses the liquidation order: bondholders and other creditors are paid before preferred stockholders.
distractorExplanations.a: Preferred holders are paid before common and usually cannot vote.
distractorExplanations.c: Preferred dividends are usually fixed; common dividends vary with earnings.

options.a: Bond price sensitivity to rate changes
options.b: Time remaining until a bond matures
options.c: A stock's sensitivity to the market
options.d: Default risk reflected in a bond's credit spread

distractorExplanations.d: Credit spread and default risk measure issuer quality; duration measures price sensitivity to interest-rate changes.
distractorExplanations.b: Maturity is a date; duration weights the timing of all cash flows.
distractorExplanations.c: Sensitivity of a stock to the market is beta.

options.a: A foreign share traded on its home exchange
options.b: A U.S. company's shares sold to foreign buyers
options.c: A U.S.-traded receipt for foreign company shares
options.d: A fund that holds a basket of foreign stocks

distractorExplanations.a: An ADR trades in the U.S., not on the foreign home exchange.
distractorExplanations.b: ADRs represent foreign issuers' shares, not U.S. companies'.
distractorExplanations.d: A basket of foreign stocks is a fund, while an ADR represents one issuer.

options.a: Up to 13 months, and it can be backdated 90 days
options.b: Up to 12 months, and it cannot be backdated
options.c: Up to 24 months, and it can be backdated 30 days
options.d: Up to 6 months, and it can be backdated 60 days

distractorExplanations.b: The standard LOI window is 13 months, and it can be backdated up to 90 days.
distractorExplanations.c: 24 months is too long; the window is 13 months.
distractorExplanations.d: Six months is too short; the window is 13 months with a 90-day backdate.

options.a: Investing a lump sum when prices look low
options.b: Buying the same number of shares at regular intervals
options.c: Selling a fixed dollar amount each month
options.d: Investing a fixed dollar amount at intervals

distractorExplanations.b: A fixed share count is not DCA; DCA invests a fixed dollar amount, so more shares are bought when prices are low.
distractorExplanations.a: Buying on perceived lows is market timing.
distractorExplanations.c: Fixed withdrawals are a systematic withdrawal plan.

options.a: Reduce unsystematic risk through low correlation
options.b: Eliminate systematic market risk by holding many securities
options.c: Raise expected return without adding risk
options.d: Replace the need to set an asset allocation

distractorExplanations.b: Diversification cannot remove systematic (market) risk; it reduces only unsystematic, company-specific risk.
distractorExplanations.c: Diversification improves risk-adjusted return but does not raise return for free.
distractorExplanations.d: Diversification works within an allocation; it does not replace one.

options.a: The client's age as the single deciding factor
options.b: The client's past returns in other accounts
options.c: The risk level of the adviser's model portfolio
options.d: Willingness and ability to take risk, plus goals

distractorExplanations.a: Age matters, but it is only one input.
distractorExplanations.b: Past returns do not show willingness or capacity to bear losses.
distractorExplanations.c: The model's risk describes the product, not the client.

options.a: Everyone pays the same percentage of income
options.b: Tax rates fall as taxable income rises
options.c: Taxes are based on spending, not income
options.d: Marginal rates rise as taxable income rises

distractorExplanations.a: One rate for all income levels is a flat tax.
distractorExplanations.b: Falling rates as income rises is a regressive system.
distractorExplanations.c: Taxes on spending are consumption taxes, such as sales taxes.

options.a: Buys more of the best performers to add momentum
options.b: Changes target weights to follow market trends
options.c: Sells winners and buys laggards to reset targets
options.d: Moves the full portfolio to cash after losses

distractorExplanations.a: Adding to winners increases drift from targets, the opposite of rebalancing.
distractorExplanations.b: Rebalancing restores existing targets; it does not chase trends.
distractorExplanations.d: Moving to cash after losses is market timing, not rebalancing.

options.a: After the first trade, along with the trade confirmation
options.b: Within 30 days after the account is opened
options.c: At or before the recommendation, order, or account
options.d: Only when the customer asks about firm conflicts

distractorExplanations.a: Form CRS must be delivered at or before the earliest of a recommendation, order, or account opening, not with the first confirmation.
distractorExplanations.b: Delivery after account opening is too late.
distractorExplanations.d: Delivery is required to all retail investors, not only on request.

options.a: Over $10,000 in cash
options.b: Over $5,000 in cash
options.c: Over $3,000 in cash
options.d: Over $25,000 in cash

distractorExplanations.b: $5,000 is the broker-dealer SAR threshold, not the CTR threshold.
distractorExplanations.c: $3,000 relates to recordkeeping for money orders and wires, not CTRs.
distractorExplanations.d: $25,000 is not the currency transaction threshold.

options.a: At least 25% of its directors
options.b: At least 40% of its directors
options.c: At least 75% of its directors
options.d: All of its directors

distractorExplanations.a: 25% is below the 1940 Act minimum.
distractorExplanations.c: Many funds exceed 75% by practice, but the statutory floor is 40%.
distractorExplanations.d: Interested directors, such as adviser officers, may serve on the board.

options.a: More than 10 retail investors in 30 days
options.b: More than 25 retail investors in 30 days
options.c: More than 50 retail investors in 90 days
options.d: More than 100 retail investors in a year

distractorExplanations.a: Ten is not the Rule 2210 threshold.
distractorExplanations.c: The threshold is 25 retail investors within 30 days.
distractorExplanations.d: The rule uses a 30-day window and 25 investors.

options.a: Up to 100% of the vested balance with no cap
options.b: The lesser of $50,000 or 50% of the vested balance
options.c: The lesser of $10,000 or 25% of the vested balance
options.d: Only hardship amounts approved by the IRS

distractorExplanations.a: Plan loans are capped; the full balance cannot be borrowed.
distractorExplanations.c: The limits are $50,000 or 50% of vested balance, not these figures.
distractorExplanations.d: Hardship withdrawals are separate from loans and need no IRS approval.

options.a: Private-sector employer retirement plans
options.b: Retirement plans for state and local government employees
options.c: Individual retirement accounts (IRAs)
options.d: Federal government employee plans

distractorExplanations.b: Governmental plans for state and local employees are exempt from ERISA; ERISA covers private-sector employer plans.
distractorExplanations.c: IRAs are not ERISA employer plans.
distractorExplanations.d: Federal plans are governed by separate statutes, not ERISA.

options.a: Funded in a trust protected from creditors
options.b: Offered to all employees under nondiscrimination rules
options.c: An unfunded promise open to employer creditors
options.d: Tax-deductible to the employer when promised

distractorExplanations.b: Nonqualified plans are not subject to qualified-plan nondiscrimination rules and are usually offered only to select executives.
distractorExplanations.a: Assets set aside for NQDC remain subject to the employer's creditors.
distractorExplanations.d: The employer deducts the cost when benefits are paid, not when promised.

options.a: If the non-working spouse has some earned income of their own
options.b: If the couple files separate federal tax returns
options.c: If the working spouse has enough earned income
options.d: Only if the spouse is at least age 50

distractorExplanations.a: The spousal IRA exists because the non-working spouse lacks earned income; it relies on the working spouse's compensation.
distractorExplanations.b: A spousal IRA requires a married-filing-jointly return; filing separately disqualifies the contribution.
distractorExplanations.d: Age affects catch-up amounts, not eligibility.

options.a: Tax-free, since the owner already paid tax
options.b: Income-taxed, with no 10% penalty for heirs
options.c: Taxed at long-term capital gains rates to the heir
options.d: Income-taxed plus a 10% early penalty

distractorExplanations.c: Traditional IRA distributions are ordinary income to the beneficiary; capital gains rates do not apply inside IRAs.
distractorExplanations.a: Pre-tax traditional IRA money is taxed when heirs withdraw it.
distractorExplanations.d: Beneficiaries are exempt from the 10% early withdrawal penalty.

options.a: The insurer's general account with a fixed rate
options.b: Separate accounts apart from the general account
options.c: A bank trust account insured by the FDIC
options.d: Stable value contracts issued by the insurance company

distractorExplanations.d: Stable value and GIC-type contracts are fixed products backed by the insurer's general account, not the separate account.
distractorExplanations.a: The general account backs fixed products, not variable subaccounts.
distractorExplanations.c: Separate accounts are not bank accounts and are not FDIC insured.

options.a: A back-end CDSC with higher ongoing 12b-1 fees
options.b: A level load charged each year with no CDSC
options.c: A front-end load with lower ongoing 12b-1 fees
options.d: No sales charge and no 12b-1 fees at all

distractorExplanations.a: A back-end CDSC with higher 12b-1 fees describes Class B shares.
distractorExplanations.b: A level annual charge describes Class C shares.
distractorExplanations.d: No sales charge describes no-load shares, not Class A.

options.a: Lower the sales charge as the purchase grows
options.b: Raise the sales charge as the purchase grows
options.c: Apply only to purchases in a single account
options.d: Set the load by how long the shares are held

distractorExplanations.d: A charge that depends on holding period is a contingent deferred sales charge (B shares), not a front-end breakpoint.
distractorExplanations.b: Breakpoints reduce, not increase, the charge on larger purchases.
distractorExplanations.c: Family accounts can often be combined to reach breakpoints.

options.a: Market price is below the value of its holdings
options.b: Market price is above the value of its holdings
options.c: The fund is charging a sales load on purchases
options.d: The fund must buy back shares at NAV right away

distractorExplanations.b: Price above NAV is a premium, not a discount.
distractorExplanations.c: Discounts reflect market pricing, not sales loads.
distractorExplanations.d: Closed-end funds do not have to redeem shares at NAV.

options.a: Tax-free exchange of one annuity for another
options.b: Tax-free withdrawal of gains after age 59½
options.c: Conversion of an annuity into a Roth IRA
options.d: A rollover of an annuity into a 401(k) plan

distractorExplanations.b: Section 1035 concerns exchanges, not tax-free withdrawals.
distractorExplanations.c: Roth conversions are separate and taxable.
distractorExplanations.d: Section 1035 covers contract-to-contract exchanges, not plan rollovers.

options.a: Highly volatile sector funds
options.b: Investment-grade bond funds
options.c: Conservative balanced funds
options.d: Money market funds for cash

distractorExplanations.b: Investment-grade bond funds can fit an income-seeking conservative investor.
distractorExplanations.c: Conservative balanced funds may be appropriate.
distractorExplanations.d: Money market funds suit near-term cash needs.

options.a: Tax-managed or municipal bond funds
options.b: High-yield corporate bond funds
options.c: High-turnover actively managed sector funds
options.d: Real estate investment trust funds

distractorExplanations.c: High turnover realizes frequent short-term gains taxed as ordinary income, which hurts tax-sensitive taxable accounts.
distractorExplanations.b: High-yield bond interest is fully taxable.
distractorExplanations.d: REIT dividends are mostly taxed as ordinary income.

options.a: Broker-dealer registration and net capital rules
options.b: Registration and prospectus rules for new corporate issues
options.c: Trading on national securities exchanges and OTC
options.d: Mutual funds, UITs, and other investment companies

distractorExplanations.b: Registration and prospectus rules for new issues come from the Securities Act of 1933, not the Investment Company Act of 1940.
distractorExplanations.a: Broker-dealer registration falls under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934.
distractorExplanations.c: Exchange trading is regulated under the 1934 Act.

options.a: Delivered or made available at or before the sale
options.b: Delivered within 90 days after the purchase date
options.c: Delivered once a year with the fund's annual report
options.d: Delivered only to first-time fund investors

distractorExplanations.c: The annual report is a separate shareholder report; the prospectus must be delivered or available at or before the sale.
distractorExplanations.b: Delivery after 90 days is too late.
distractorExplanations.d: Every purchaser must receive a prospectus.

options.a: Content is fair, balanced, and not misleading
options.b: Content is approved by FINRA before its use
options.c: Content includes a guarantee of performance
options.d: Content is filed with the SEC before its use

distractorExplanations.b: Principal approval is internal; FINRA filing is separate.
distractorExplanations.c: Performance guarantees are prohibited.
distractorExplanations.d: Retail communications are not filed with the SEC for approval.

options.a: Registration or notice filing in the state
options.b: Full merit review of each fund offered
options.c: Approval of each sale by the administrator
options.d: No filing, since funds are federal covered

distractorExplanations.b: Mutual funds are federal covered and not subject to state merit review.
distractorExplanations.c: States do not approve individual sales.
distractorExplanations.d: States may still require notice filings and fees.

options.a: Allowed on margin the same day, like listed stocks
options.b: Subject to margin and suitability rules
options.c: Allowed only in retirement accounts
options.d: Allowed if shares are held over a year

distractorExplanations.a: Mutual fund shares are a continuous new issue and cannot be bought on margin at purchase; they can serve as collateral after 30 days.
distractorExplanations.c: Margin is not allowed in retirement accounts.
distractorExplanations.d: Holding period does not govern margin use.

options.a: Tax-free if age and holding rules are met
options.b: Taxed as ordinary income on earnings
options.c: Taxed at long-term capital gains rates on the earnings
options.d: Tax-free only if taken before age 59½

distractorExplanations.c: Qualified Roth distributions are fully tax-free; capital gains treatment applies to taxable accounts, not Roth IRAs.
distractorExplanations.b: Qualified Roth withdrawals are tax-free.
distractorExplanations.d: Qualified withdrawals generally require age 59½ or another qualifying event.

options.a: Immediately, in every plan
options.b: Per the plan's vesting schedule
options.c: After a ten-year cliff vesting period
options.d: Only when the employee retires

distractorExplanations.c: Ten-year cliff vesting is not permitted; employer 401(k) contributions must vest under a 3-year cliff or 2-to-6-year graded schedule.
distractorExplanations.a: Some plans vest immediately, but many use schedules.
distractorExplanations.d: Vesting is based on service, not retirement.

options.a: At age 59½, when penalties end
options.b: At age 65, alongside Medicare
options.c: At the IRS-required age by law
options.d: At age 70½ under current law

distractorExplanations.a: Age 59½ is when the 10% early-withdrawal penalty generally ends; RMDs start later, at the SECURE 2.0 starting age.
distractorExplanations.d: Age 70½ was the pre-2020 RMD age; SECURE and SECURE 2.0 raised it (currently 73).
distractorExplanations.b: RMD age is not tied to Medicare eligibility.

options.a: Allows contributions above annual IRS limits
options.b: Keeps tax deferral if done as a direct rollover
options.c: Converts pre-tax money into Roth money tax-free
options.d: Gives the assets FDIC insurance in the IRA

distractorExplanations.a: Rollovers do not change annual contribution limits.
distractorExplanations.c: Moving pre-tax money to a Roth is a taxable conversion.
distractorExplanations.d: IRA investments are not FDIC insured unless held in bank deposits.

options.a: Contribute without any annual dollar limit
options.b: Skip the plan's vesting schedule
options.c: Add more above standard limits after age 50
options.d: Make Roth contributions above income limits

distractorExplanations.a: Catch-up contributions have their own limits.
distractorExplanations.b: Catch-ups do not affect vesting.
distractorExplanations.d: Catch-ups do not waive Roth IRA income limits.

options.a: Higher contribution limits than the IRA
options.b: FDIC insurance on the annuity values
options.c: Extra cost, since the IRA is tax-deferred
options.d: Removal of surrender charges by law

distractorExplanations.a: IRA contribution limits apply regardless of investment.
distractorExplanations.b: Annuities are not FDIC insured.
distractorExplanations.d: Surrender charges can still apply inside IRAs.

options.a: Public school and 501(c)(3) employees
options.b: Employees of any for-profit company
options.c: State and local government workers
options.d: Self-employed individuals only

distractorExplanations.b: For-profit employers use 401(k) plans.
distractorExplanations.c: State and local governments generally use 457 plans.
distractorExplanations.d: Self-employed individuals use SEP IRAs or solo 401(k)s.

options.a: May be repeated as often as the owner likes
options.b: Takes 60 days; one per 12 months across IRAs
options.c: Takes 90 days; one per calendar year per IRA
options.d: Is exempt from any timing or frequency rules

distractorExplanations.a: Indirect rollovers are limited to one per 12 months.
distractorExplanations.c: The window is 60 days, and the limit applies across all IRAs.
distractorExplanations.d: Indirect rollovers are subject to the 60-day and once-a-year rules.
